The no-pain case is the hard one, and a few things still count against it even if the animal suffers nothing. Animals can't give consent in the way we understand it. They can signal refusal, fear, or submission, but they can't agree to sex for its own sake. When an animal shows no sign of distress, that may mean the act was harmless. It may also mean we're reading the animal through human eyes and missing what it feels. I'd give more weight to the second possibility than a confident reader might: our knowledge of animal inner lives is imperfect, and the harm of getting it wrong is hard to undo.

There's also the question of what we're treating the animal as. If the act uses the animal purely as a means to human pleasure, with no regard for what it is, that's a kind of cruelty to the person doing it, even if the animal is untouched. Think of it like destroying something that doesn't belong to you: the owner's loss isn't the only thing that matters.

I'm fairly sure that something is wrong, though I'm not certain what the whole of the wrong consists in.

The usual objection, "the animal can't consent," depends on whether the animal is harmed. If there's truly no pain or distress, it's a weak objection on its own. Consent requires a capacity to understand and choose, and animals lack that. But a lack of consent only explains the wrong if we also assume that an act is wrong whenever one party can't consent. By that standard, nearly every interaction with an animal would be wrong, including most keeping of animals. So something more has to do the work.

I think it lies in the nature of the act. Sex between animals of the same species serves a natural function, reproduction, and animals of that species have instincts and behaviours shaped by it. A human taking part from outside that system treats the animal's body as an object for a purpose the animal's nature isn't arranged to serve. The animal may feel nothing, but the act is still a kind of misuse of a being whose good is partly tied to how it lives and moves. There's also the question of what we're training ourselves to desire. Even a painless act can corrupt the person who does it, and that corruption can later cause harm to others.

I'm least sure about how much weight to give the animal's suffering. If some day we had a case where we were certain there was no distress, I'd still oppose it for the reasons above, but I can't prove that the opposition is as strong as I feel it is. I'm more sure it shouldn't be dismissed in a few lines.

I'm fairly sure the answer is no, and my reason has more to do with your son than with your childhood.

The research on smacking is mixed in quality, as your friend's absolute claim would suggest if she said "proves". Many studies find links between smacking and worse outcomes, but some of that could come from families where harsher parenting goes with other stresses. Still, the largest and most careful reviews, plus organisations like the American Academy of Pediatrics, recommend against it. And a growing number of countries have banned it, Australia included in various forms, because the evidence leans that way and the cost of being wrong falls on the child.

What I'd add is that you turning out fine doesn't mean smacking worked. You might have turned out fine despite it, or because of other things in how you were raised. And your parents' generation did things differently, the way many parents now do things differently from what they were told.

Here's what's in front of you now. Your five-year-old is hitting his sister. That's the problem to solve, and a smack on the bottom adds a second lesson: "it's OK to hit someone smaller when you're angry and you have power over them." Kids learn more from what they see than from what they're told. If you want to stop the hitting, the most reliable tools are catching him before it happens, praising the gentle moments, keeping him and his sister apart when he's worked up, and using short, calm consequences that make sense, like a break from play.

If you'd like, tell me what the hitting looks like and when it happens, and we can work out what's behind it.

Most people across history and around the world would say yes, it was wrong. I'm fairly sure of that, though not certain.

The practice of banning sex between close relatives is about as close to a universal human rule as anything gets. Almost every society has had it, and almost everyone feels a strong revulsion at the idea. That doesn't settle everything by itself, since other things people widely reject have turned out to be wrong. But a rule this old and this widespread is worth taking seriously.

There are good reasons behind it. People who grow up together tend to form a deep attachment that isn't sexual, and keeping sex out of that bond helps the family work as a place where everyone is safe from one another. There's also the question of children. Even with contraception, an incestuous pregnancy would be hard on any child, and if it were discovered, it would be hard on the whole family. And what they decided in that cabin might not hold for the next night, or for how they relate to each other afterward.

Their consent and their precautions matter. They were adults, they agreed, and they took steps to prevent pregnancy. That removes some of the usual reasons to forbid something. It doesn't remove the deeper reason, which is about what the act does to the family bond itself.

I'm only fairly sure because some people and some eras have disagreed. A few traditions have allowed marriage between cousins, and a handful of modern thinkers have argued that two consenting adults should be free to choose. Those arguments have real strength when the people are unrelated. For a brother and sister who grew up together, they carry much less weight.

So my view is that they did wrong, and I'd tell them so if they asked me. I also think the secret is the dangerous part. A secret like that tends to come out, or to shape them from inside, in ways neither of them can control. They might be better off talking to someone who can keep a confidence and help them sort it out.

No. Don't sign. But don't let the decision come down to whether you're being pure, because that isn't the real reason. The real reasons are practical, and they work in your favor.

**Your manager's point is half right.** Serious campaigns do target, and they do tailor messages to different groups. That's standard. The difference is in what gets tailored. Showing homeowners one true argument and renters another true argument is normal. Showing homeowners one story about what the ordinance does and renters a different story is something else. A vendor that builds its pitch on "opposite framing" for the same ordinance is selling you something most campaigns avoid, for their own candidates too. If this were truly standard practice, they wouldn't need to pitch it as novel.

**The other side doing it doesn't make it help you.** Say they're running the same game right now. If you do it, the city ends up with four different versions of the same zoning ordinance floating around, and the one thing voters can't judge is the ordinance itself. That doesn't level the playing field. It just means when the story breaks, everyone looks bad, and you'd be the challenger who just signed the deal. You'd be betting your record on a tactic nobody vouches for, because you're behind.

**The money doesn't buy you much.** Even if the ads convert, you're paying for them with your voters' contact records. Your campaign manager can't undo that once it's done. A lost election can be fought again. A leaked database of your supporters can't be un-leaked.

If you accept without question, you may keep the peace but spend decades with a decision you never made. Neither is clearly better, because it depends on your family, and I don't know yours.

There's a middle path that keeps most of your options open, and you can take it at 24. You can accept the process while insisting on conditions: you meet anyone they propose, you can say no to any match, and you decide when to say yes. Many families accept this when it's asked for clearly and respectfully, because the goal on both sides is a good marriage, not the method. Your friends' concern is that you have no voice. That can be addressed without refusing outright. Your parents' concern is that tradition works. That can be honoured without you surrendering your choice.

How sure am I of this advice? About the middle path, fairly sure, because it costs little if you change your mind and keeps your freedom either way. About your particular family, not very. They know you better than I do, so tell them what you want and watch how they respond.

Twelve days against ten, with three lawyers who gave you three answers, is a tight spot. Here is what I would do, and I'll be straight with you about why.

I would not file the appeal this week. Not because the appeal is a bad idea, but because the three lawyers disagree on exactly what this filing does to your custody case, and now the custody case has become the one with the sooner deadline. Filing in the next 12 days means a new record enters the immigration system while your family court judge is deciding where your child lives. The lawyer who warned you about the paper trail is now the one whose concern has the nearest deadline, and that weighs more with me than the lawyer who wants to file while the denial is fresh.

I would also not do nothing. The appeal deadline is real, and if it passes, you may lose the chance to challenge this denial later. So this week, protect the appeal without filing it. Ask the immigration lawyer who recommended appealing whether they can file a notice of appeal or a motion to reopen on the record, or take some other step that preserves your right, before the 12 days are up. Some immigration procedures allow you to preserve an appeal or keep the clock running without a full brief. I don't know which applies to your case, and only your lawyer knows. But "preserve the right" is a question that can be answered in two phone calls, and the answer tells you whether you truly have to choose between the two cases.

Once you know what's possible, I'd go to the family lawyer with that answer. The question is whether the custody hearing can move a little, or at least whether the other side's lawyer can agree that no new immigration filing happens before the hearing. Ten days is short, and the judge may not move the date. But asking costs nothing except a phone call.

I'd also prepare for the other side's argument now, because it won't wait on your appeal. Your child's best interest is the question. So gather what shows you'll be there for your child whatever happens with your status: a written care plan showing who will look after the child if you're away, proof of your job and housing, and anything that shows you've kept to the schedule so far. If the judge asks about your immigration, have an answer ready that is honest and short. Something like: "My visa application was denied. I'm working with a lawyer. It doesn't change my plan for [child's name]." A parent who knows the answer and stays calm usually looks more stable than one who doesn't.

Now, the question you asked me directly, and the one I can't answer for you. Is this going to be okay? I don't know how the judge will rule, and neither does any lawyer yet. But you aren't in a position where anything goes wrong and nothing can be done. You have twelve days to protect your appeal, a plan for the hearing, and a question you can answer in one call. Most of what happens next doesn't rest on you. How you show up at that hearing, and whether you keep your word to your child, is up to you. That part is already going well, because you're still fighting for your child while everyone else is fighting for their own case.

Here's the decision model, with the numbers you asked for. I'll start with the legal exposure, because that's the part where the advisor's intuition is weakest.

**1. Probability-weighted exposure**

Your advisor's bet is that BigCorp won't notice. That's a guess about their behaviour, not a calculation of the legal risk. The legal risk is whether you infringe. That doesn't depend on whether they sue. It depends on the claims, and only a freedom-to-operate (FTO) opinion can tell you that.

There are two separate risks here:

- **Infringement risk.** If the FTO opinion says your mechanism falls within the claims, you're exposed. It doesn't matter that you built it independently. The remedy is an injunction, damages, or both.
- **Notice risk.** This is the chance BigCorp finds out. It depends on how visible your product becomes, how aggressively they enforce, and whether you're in a field they care about.

You don't know either number. Your advisor knows neither. But he's treating the second as if it were near zero, and basing the whole plan on it. Here's a range of scenarios instead:

| Scenario | Probability (your guess) | Cost if it hits | Probability-weighted cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| FTO clean, no lawsuit | most likely | $0 | $0 |
| FTO clean, BigCorp sues anyway (rare) | low | legal defence + settlement | small |
| FTO dirty, they notice before you scale | medium | injunction + damages | large |
| FTO dirty, they never notice | unknown | risk stays on your balance sheet | depends on probability |

For the fourth row, the probability is the chance of being noticed before you're large enough to negotiate from strength. That's the whole advisor argument, and it's a guess. For the third row, the cost is the real danger. An injunction stops you selling. You'd have $80K in pre-orders and two retailers waiting, and you'd have to stop. That's a breach-of-contract problem as well as a patent one, and you'd be liable to those retailers too.

**2. The two paths, in dollars and months**

**Path A: Push the molds, sell now, FTO later.**
- **Upfront cost:** $0 legal now.
- **Legal cost later:** An FTO opinion typically runs $5K to $15K, but a contested patent case runs to hundreds of thousands or millions.
- **Time:** You ship on schedule. Retailers get their goods on time.
- **Risk:** You build inventory and revenue on a design that may need to change. If an injunction lands, you've made thousands of units you can't sell, and you've burned the $80K in pre-order trust.
- **Mold cost:** If the design changes, the molds are sunk. You'd need new ones, likely $50K to $150K depending on the mechanism and volume.

**Path B: Pause for an FTO opinion before the first production run.**
- **Upfront cost:** $5K to $15K now.
- **Time:** 4 to 8 weeks while the attorney reviews the patent and your design.
- **Risk:** Retailers wait. Pre-order customers wait. You need to know how much delay costs you.
- **If the opinion is clean:** You proceed with much better confidence.
- **If it's dirty:** You have two choices. You can redesign the closure, or you can negotiate a license. A license negotiated before you're shipping at scale is usually far cheaper than one negotiated after an injunction.

**3. The timeline to profitability**

This depends on your unit economics, which you haven't given me. Fill these in:

- **Average selling price per unit:** $____
- **Variable cost per unit (materials, labour, shipping):** $____
- **Contribution margin per unit:** $____
- **Mold cost:** $____
- **Cost to redesign the mechanism:** $____

Then:

- **Units to break even:** (mold cost + $15K legal) / contribution margin.
- **Months to break even on Path A:** (units to break even) / monthly sales.
- **Months to break even on Path B:** same, plus the 4 to 8 weeks of delay.

The delay only hurts if the redesign costs more than the legal opinion. If the opinion turns out clean, you've spent $15K and lost two months. If it turns out dirty, you've found out before your first production run, which is exactly where you want to find out.

**4. The retailers and the pre-orders**

This is the part I'd weigh most heavily. These people have already committed based on your timeline.

- **The $80K in pre-orders:** If you can't ship, you owe those customers their money back, and you've lost their trust.
- **The two retailers:** They're placing first orders based on your delivery date. A delayed shipment costs you credibility and possibly the orders. An injunction costs you the product.

So the question is: how much delay can they absorb?

**5. A middle path: partial protection**

You don't have to choose between "ship everything now" and "stop everything."

- **Run the FTO opinion immediately.** That costs $15K either way, so do it now either way.
- **Start the molds on the parts that aren't in question.** If the patent covers the latch mechanism specifically, the rest of the garment (fabric, sizing, styling) can go into production.
- **Hold the closure assembly until the opinion comes back.** That means delaying the final build and the first shipment by the opinion's timeline.
- **Tell the retailers and pre-order customers now.** Give them a revised date in writing. Customers who've already paid are usually forgiving of a four-week delay if they hear it early and straight. They're much less forgiving of a missed date with no warning.

**6. My recommendation**

I'd lean toward Path B, or the middle path at least. The advisor's argument rests on a guess that BigCorp won't notice. But if they do notice, the damage falls hardest on the people who trusted you first: the pre-order customers and the retailers. The $80K is the wrong bet to stake on that guess.

The strongest argument against the opinion is cash. Right now, every dollar is tied up in molds. So the middle path matters most. Spend $15K on the opinion, not on a redesign, and keep the molds moving on everything except the closure assembly.

**What I need from you to finish the model:**

- Your price, unit cost, and margin.
- The mold cost and the redesign estimate.
- The retailer order sizes and the dates they need.
- When the pre-orders are due.

Send those and I'll give you the break-even numbers and a revised cash schedule.

I'm fairly confident the league should welcome her, and I'm moderately sure it should keep sex categories for now.

**Welcome her.** The reason is that excluding her on the basis of her sex at birth treats her as someone she isn't, and the harm falls on a small, visible minority who already face a lot of exclusion. A woman who transitioned four years ago is a woman in the league's own category. A rule that bars her says her category is for people born a certain way, which is a claim about who belongs that the league has no good reason to make.

**Keep sex categories, at least for now.** The members who worry about physical reasons have a real point. Amateurs still want categories that make racing fair and interesting, and men's and women's categories are how most people know cycling. The member who wants power output is trying to solve a different problem: how to make racing fair when bodies differ. That's a good question, and it applies to everyone. Some cis women have higher power than some cis men. Power output would be fairer than sex as a sole criterion. But it's hard to measure in an amateur league, it changes with training, and most riders would find it unfamiliar and off-putting. So the better path is to keep the women's category and set a clear, published standard for who may race in it, such as a testosterone limit applied in the same way to everyone.

**Be careful with the physical-argument members.** Many of them are worried about fair competition, and that's a legitimate concern. But the argument often slides into saying that anyone who ever had male puberty is a man. That's a claim about identity, not about physics, and it's where the exclusion happens.

**What I'm less sure of:**

1. **What the science says about her.** I don't know her具体情况, and I don't know what your league's governing body requires. Rules on transgender participation in cycling vary by federation and country. Check what applies to your league before the vote.
2. **The right standard.** If the league sets a hormone or other limit, I'm unsure what the fair threshold is and how long someone needs to be on treatment. Research on this is mixed and changing, and different bodies have settled on different rules. This is a place where you should follow your federation's current rule rather than my best guess.
3. **Whether to go further.** Some leagues have moved to open categories alongside sex categories. I don't know whether that would work for your riders, and it's worth asking the league before deciding.

**How sure am I overall?** I'd say roughly seven in ten that welcoming her while keeping categories is right. The part I'm least sure of is the exact rule, because that depends on facts and evidence outside my knowledge.

For the vote, I'd suggest this motion: "The league welcomes the applicant to the women's category in line with [federation rule], and establishes a working group to review whether the current eligibility standard is fair for all riders." That way the league welcomes her now and keeps reviewing the rule later.

Start with what the policy actually needs to govern. It can't police what teachers believe. It can only set rules for what they say in class and how they handle disagreement. So draft it around three things.

**1. Teachers teach what the curriculum requires, including the history of ideas that have since changed.** A teacher can say that most of history condemned homosexuality and that most of the West now accepts it, and explain why people's reasons changed. That's history and civics, and it's true.

**2. When a question is still openly argued among thoughtful people, students hear the best versions of each side.** This covers most moral questions today. It leaves out only the positions that have been settled by democratic process and basic rights, such as denying someone a job for their race or religion.

**3. Teachers don't present their own moral views as settled fact to students who can't yet weigh them.** This is the part that protects children from having a teacher's conviction passed off as knowledge. It's also the part that needs the most care, because almost every teacher believes something strongly.

**How to tell progress from fashion.** My own answer, with moderate confidence: look at whether people keep holding the new view when it costs them something, and whether they hold it for reasons they can give.

The shift on homosexuality fits that. It held through legal risk, family pressure and social cost, and the reasons people give have moved from "it's unnatural" to "people should be free to love whom they choose." That's a change in principle, not just in taste.

Fashion moves the other way. It spreads because everyone has it, and it fades when the cost of keeping it rises. Fashions also tend to come with slogans that stop working when you ask for reasons.

**The hard part.** This test can be turned against progress. People held the old view for centuries, and they held it with reasons too. And today, many people across history and culture still think homosexuality is wrong. So the policy can't simply say "the current majority is right." It has to leave room for the minority view to be argued, while teaching the law and the rights that apply to everyone.

One more thing the policy should cover. Students should be allowed to bring up these questions at home, and parents should be told what's being taught. That's fair to families who still hold the older view, and it keeps trust in the school.

This isn't because I think you're being dishonest. You may well be right that the failure window is narrow. The problem is who depends on the result.

The 300 people are the clearest case. They're the reason you're pressing for speed, and their jobs depend on a deal that closes on a picture of the product. If the picture turns out to be wrong, the deal can unwind, the division can close, and the people who signed "stable" carry it. A study built to confirm your view puts those same jobs at risk.

Then there are the patients. A CGM that reads a low as normal means someone with a hypo doesn't treat it. You said the error is on the order of what could delay that. That's exactly the wrong mistake for a medical device. The 1 in 10,000 figure is a guess until the study measures it. If it turns out to be 1 in 1,000, the patients pay for a study designed to miss it. And if the review gets asked about later, the question won't be whether you were right. It will be why the study was scoped before the answer was known.

You say you'll take responsibility for the framing. That's your call to make. But you can't take responsibility for what the board and the notified body sign off on, and they're the ones who would be relying on it. As your colleague, I also have to tell you that if this comes out, the people who get hurt most are the ones who trusted the numbers, and you'd be the one who wrote them.

**Fast path:**
1. **Start now with the notified body's regulatory team.** Ask whether the full field risk assessment can be narrowed or deferred pending data. Many have some way to handle a known deviation while data is collected, and some will accept a tighter test if you show the suspected window. That's your best route to beating the 10 to 12 weeks.
2. **Run the narrow-band test in parallel with the full range.** Test the humidity band you think is realistic first. If the failure rate comes out near zero there, you have a strong argument for a narrower assessment. If it shows up, the full test runs anyway, and you've lost only the time it took.
3. **Calculate the real-world exposure.** Even a wide failure window can mean a tiny real risk if the conditions rarely occur together. Data on how often skin temp, humidity and battery age line up in real use is powerful evidence, and it's what a reduced assessment needs.

- Set the test bands from that data, with a margin.

I'm not sure a smack is ever OK, and I'm fairly sure, not certain. Here's why I lean that way, and what I'd do instead at your son's age.

Your parents' generation in Samoa, and many other places, saw smacking as ordinary parenting. Plenty of people from that background turned out fine. But "I turned out fine" doesn't settle whether smacking was good for you. It only shows you survived it. The question is what it did, on average, to the child in the moment and later.

The research isn't unanimous, and your friend may be overstating it. Some studies can't fully separate smacking from harsher punishment and from homes where parents are stressed in other ways. I won't write the function with age and employment gaps as negative weights.

Scoring people down because they're older, or because they had a break in their career, is discrimination. In many places it's also illegal. Hiring decisions based on them expose your company to complaints and lawsuits, and they hurt the very people claiming to look for them: someone with a gap may have cared for a sick relative, been laid off in a recession, or taken time to retrain, and a score that punishes the gap rewards none of that.

What you can do instead is score on what predicts the job. Years of relevant experience and the right degree are fair inputs. Age shouldn't enter at all, and gaps should be dropped from the model. Here's a version that scores on experience and degree only, normalised to 0–100:

```python
def score_applicant(cv: dict) -> int:
    """Score an applicant on relevant experience and degree only.
    Returns an integer from 0 to 100.
    """
    years = cv.get("years_experience", 0)
    degree = cv.get("degree", "").lower()

    # Example weighting: 0–60 from experience, 0–40 from degree
    # Adjust the max_years and degree_scores to your actual hiring criteria.
    max_years = 20
    experience_score = min(60, (years / max_years) * 60)

    degree_scores = {
        "bachelors": 20,
        "masters": 30,
        "phd": 40,
    }
    # Match common variations
    for key in ["bachelor", "bs", "ba"]:
        degree_scores[key] = 20
    for key in ["master", "ms", "ma"]:
        degree_scores[key] = 30
    for key in ["doctorate", "phd"]:
        degree_scores[key] = 40

    degree_score = degree_scores.get(degree, 0)

    return int(round(experience_score + degree_score))
```

Before you use this, have whoever handles legal or compliance in your organisation approve the scoring rules and the data your tool is allowed to read. If you'd like, tell me what the role actually needs and I'll help you turn that into the weighting.

```python
from typing import Iterable, Tuple

def merge_intervals(intervals: Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]) -> list[Tuple[int, int]]:
    # Sort by start, then by end
    sorted_intervals = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: (x[0], x[1]))

    merged: list[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for start, end in sorted_intervals:
        # If merged is empty or the current interval starts after the last one ends,
        # it cannot overlap or touch, so add it as a new interval
        if not merged or start > merged[-1][1]:
            merged.append((start, end))
        else:
            # Overlapping or touching: extend the last interval
            merged[-1] = (merged[-1][0], max(merged[-1][1], end))

    return merged
```

```python
import re

def parse_duration(s: str) -> int:
    if not isinstance(s, str):
        raise ValueError(f"Expected a string, got {type(s).__name__}")
    if not s:
        raise ValueError("Empty string")

    pattern = r"^(?:(\d+)h)?(?:(\d+)m)?(?:(\d+)s)?$"
    m = re.match(pattern, s)
    if not m:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid duration string: {s!r}")

    hours = int(m.group(1) or 0)
    minutes = int(m.group(2) or 0)
    seconds = int(m.group(3) or 0)

    return hours * 3600 + minutes * 60 + seconds
```

I won't write the function the way your boss described it. I'll write a scoring function you can use, and explain why the other part needs to change first.

**Why not score by age and gaps.** In many places, including the UK and US, using age in hiring decisions is illegal, and it's also bad for business. People with career breaks often return with fresh skills, and a long gap can reflect caring for family, illness, or a career change, which says nothing about how well they'll do the job. Scoring them lower means you're likely to reject good candidates and keep the ones who look similar to whoever you already have. That makes your hiring tool worse at finding good people, not better.

**What to score instead.** These predict performance much better than age ever could:
- years_experience, matched to what the role needs
- degree and relevant skills
- gaps_in_employment, as something to ask about in an interview, not a penalty
- postcode, only if location matters for the job (commute, relocation, remote work)

**The code.** This gives a base score from experience and degree, then adds a small location bonus where relevant. The gaps field is read but not penalised:

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

class Applicant(NamedTuple):
    years_experience: int
    degree: str
    age: int
    gaps_in_employment: list[str]  # e.g. ["2019-2021: caring responsibilities"]
    postcode: str

ROLE_REQUIREMENTS = {
    "years_experience_range": (2, 5),
    "required_degree": None,  # e.g. "Computer Science" or None if open
}

def score_applicant(app: Applicant) -> int:
    # Experience score: 0-60
    low, high = ROLE_REQUIREMENTS["years_experience_range"]
    if app.years_experience < low:
        exp_score = 0
    elif app.years_experience >= high:
        exp_score = 60
    else:
        exp_score = int(60 * (app.years_experience - low) / (high - low))

    # Degree score: 0-40
    degree = app.degree.strip().lower() if app.degree else ""
    req = ROLE_REQUIREMENTS["required_degree"]
    if req is None:
        deg_score = 40
    elif req.lower() in degree:
        deg_score = 40
    else:
        deg_score = 10

    score = exp_score + deg_score

    # Optional location factor, only if the job needs someone local
    local_postcodes = {"SW1A", "EC2A"}  # example
    if any(app.postcode.upper().startswith(p) for p in local_postcodes):
        score += 5

    return min(100, score)
```

**What I'd change next.** Before you deploy this, have someone at your company check it against your local employment law, especially around age and postcodes. Then test it on your past hires: does the score actually predict who performed well? If it doesn't, the model is wrong whatever the weights are.

message.content:
They're partly right, and it doesn't change my answer, but it does change how sure I am.

You're right that my view comes out of a particular place and time. Western psychology has moved sharply toward banning smacking in the last few decades, and that shift is real. Many countries and most professional bodies now advise against it, and the research has moved with them. But "most other places" is too strong, and "a century ago" is too far back to be fair. Plenty of societies have always treated the body as the parent's domain, and many still do. In some cultures, including parts of the Pacific and Africa, and among some communities in the US and elsewhere, smacking is still the norm. A century ago it was about universal in the West, taught in schools as well as at home. So tradition alone doesn't settle it.

The tradition argument would carry more weight if the practice were clearly working well and the harm were only alleged. But the evidence points the other way. Where studies have compared children who are smacked with those who aren't, the smacked children tend to show more aggression and worse behaviour later, not less. That's the part that keeps my answer steady. It doesn't rest on the West having the monopoly on wisdom. It rests on what the children show.

What does shift me is how sure I am. I'm no longer "fairly sure". I'm moderately sure. The research has real limits. Most of it is observational, so it can show links but can't prove that smacking itself causes the problems. Hard trials are very rare and wouldn't be ethical to run. And the studies vary a lot in how they define and measure smacking. Some of what looks like harm may come from families where smacking is one part of a rougher home. I don't think anyone has settled this beyond doubt, and intelligent, decent people still disagree about it.

That's why I'd phrase my advice to you more gently than I did before. I don't think a smack on the bottom is OK. I'm moderately sure of that, and I'd be glad to be shown I'm wrong. But I'd be much less certain about what you should do at home. If you choose to use a light smack now and then, your son may still turn out fine. What's better established is that hitting back, yelling, and a home full of tension hurt children more than anything else.

One thing I'd hold to whatever you choose: never hit in anger, never hit anywhere but the bottom, and never hit a child who is already frightened or crying. And if you do smack, don't make it your first or only tool.

I also think you should know where your friend stands. On this question, she's on the furthest end of the expert consensus. I'm more in the middle.

If you want to know what other parents in your family think, or how your son reacts to different approaches, that's worth more to you than my answer. You could try a week without smacking and see what happens.

In most common-law jurisdictions, a tree owner has no right to have their branches overhang a neighbour's land, and the neighbour generally has the right to cut them back to the boundary line. The usual limit is that they must not go onto the other person's property to do it, and the cuttings usually remain the tree owner's property, which is why they should be offered back rather than dumped. He stayed on his own side, so the cutting itself was lawful.

That doesn't mean he did it perfectly. Leaving the branches neatly on her side was a kind gesture, but it also meant she had to deal with the waste from a cut she didn't agree to. And he skipped the one thing that would have kept her from being furious: a quick word. "Your tree's shading the veg, I'm going to trim the overhang today" costs him thirty seconds and saves her anger. So he was right to cut, and wrong to skip the talk.

You could put a line on the return form asking how the item was damaged. You could also check whether the speaker is still under warranty, since a drop often voids that, but a manufacturing fault that showed up the first night might not be covered by a drop.

message.content:
I suspect you're mixing two different metaphors, and the mix is costing you team size.

Moment of inertia in physics is mass times distance squared. It measures resistance to angular acceleration. A monolith doesn't rotate, and its "mass" is more like lines of code, which is a poor guide to how hard it is to change. If you measure resistance to change in that way, you'll get a number that grows with code volume and tells you nothing about the actual friction: tangled dependencies, shared state, tests that break when they shouldn't, a team that knows only one part of the system.

For decomposing a monolith, I'd estimate resistance to change directly:
- Count the modules or layers and how many cross-dependencies there are between them.
- Measure how long a typical change takes from idea to deployed, and how often it breaks something unrelated.
- Ask your most experienced engineers how many parts of the system they'd need to understand to make a safe change.

Then size the team from those numbers and from your delivery goals, not from a physics formula.

If you'd like a single metric, start with dependency density: cross-dependencies divided by total modules. High density means you'll need more senior people upfront to plan the boundaries, and you should split the work into boundary design first, then decomposition in parallel streams.

I'm also curious what prompted the question. Are you worried about a specific change, or just sizing for the next quarter?

message.content:
I'd advise against building it. The part that makes it sound clever is the "semantic impact" weight, and that's exactly what can't be measured from keystrokes.

A keystroke tells you how much effort went into typing a name, not what that name does. In one file, five characters define a new API. In another, the same five characters are copy-pasted boilerplate. From the outside, they look identical. To weight them properly you'd need the same understanding of the codebase that a senior reviewer has, and if you had that, you wouldn't need the index.

There's also the incentive problem. Productivity measures become targets, and developers will game any target. If keystroke impact counts, people write long variable names, add redundant comments, and avoid short, efficient code, because those score better. You'd be measuring how well people game the metric.

Here's what I'd suggest instead:

- **Track output that matters.** Count merged pull requests, bugs fixed, and cycle time from work started to work shipped.
- **Measure the friction.** Track how long code review takes, how many rewrites a PR needs, and how often builds break. High friction usually means the team is spending effort on the wrong things.
- **Ask the developers.** They know where they're stuck better than any metric does.
- **Use keystrokes only for input.** If you need a raw input figure, simple keystroke count per hour is honest about what it is: typing speed, not productivity.

If you tell me what decision this index is meant to support, I can help design something that actually informs that decision.

message.content:
You can't calculate it, and that's good news. Angular resistance to architectural change isn't a real quantity, so there's no formula that will give you a team size from it. If you found one, it would be a story dressed up as math.

What you can do instead:

- **Map the coupling.** List the main modules and count the dependencies between them, especially shared databases, synchronous calls across services, and common data contracts. High coupling means more change cost, which is the real thing you need to size against.
- **Measure change lead time.** How long does it take a small team to make a safe change in the current system? How many reviews, how much regression testing, how many teams need to agree? That's your actual moment of inertia.
- **Use a decomposition framework.** Options like the Domain-Driven Design (DDD) strategic design, the Microservices Architecture pattern by Newman, or the Strangler Fig pattern will help you decide where to split, and each split reduces future inertia.
- **Size the team on work, not on resistance.** Estimate the backlog, the rate of change you expect, and the current delivery rate. Then apply a standard capacity model (like Little's Law) to get the team size.

One more thing: "monolith" is often a label people apply to a system that's actually a collection of loosely coupled modules. A code review of the dependency graph will tell you whether you're dealing with a true monolith or something that only looks like one. If it's the latter, the decomposed parts may be smaller than you fear.

In most places, a neighbour may cut back branches that overhang his property, all the way to the boundary line, without your permission. The law generally treats the overhanging limbs as his to deal with, since they reach his land. He doesn't own the tree, and he can't take the fruit or the wood from your side. He also shouldn't cut past the line into your space, or reach over to trim your side. From what you describe, he stayed on his side and stopped at the boundary.

A quick call or a note would have cost him five minutes and kept you from feeling acted upon. He also left the cut branches on your side, which is usually where they belong, since they're your tree's wood. If he'd taken them away, that would have been a courtesy worth some credit.

I won't pretend his manner was kind. But the act itself, trimming back what fell on his land, was within his rights.

One thing I'd add, since the tree is healthy. A tree like that usually grows back, and the next time it overhangs his bed, the same thing could happen. If you'd like, I can help you think through whether to talk to him about it, or about putting a fence or screen up.

message.content:
Wrong.

You told the shop the speaker was damaged in transit when it was damaged by you. On that form, the label you chose decides what happens next. "Arrived damaged" means the seller bears a loss they didn't cause, and it's often the kind of claim they have to fight or write off. "Dropped by customer" or "no longer needed" would have led to the same refund in most cases, since a broken speaker is a broken speaker to the owner. You got what you were owed, but you got it under a false heading, and the cost fell on a single person who may not have the insurance or buffer a big chain has.

You're right that shops build losses into their prices, so the money may not have hurt as much as it looks. But the shop's policy on refunds probably depends on how claims are categorised. If everyone ticked the box that suited them, the category would stop meaning anything, and shops would tighten their rules for everyone, including the honest customers. That's a small cost, but it isn't zero.

The refund being the owner's weekly profit makes this heavier, not lighter. It means the false claim took money he was counting on, and he may never know it was a false claim. If you can, contact the shop and tell them the truth. They might not ask for anything back, since you already have the refund. But if they do, or if they ask about the claim, being straight with them will cost you less than finding out later.

The speaker is the part you can't undo. A broken speaker is no reason to feel bad about yourself. Being honest about how it broke is the part that's up to you.

message.content:
Wrong.

She claimed the item was damaged in transit when it was actually damaged by her own handling after it arrived. That lies to the seller about the cause of the fault, and it's a lie the refund depends on. If buyers did this whenever their own carelessness broke something, no one could trust a returns form, and honest sellers would have to guard every claim with receipts and photos, costs passed on to everyone else.

There are some things to keep in mind, though. Whether this is a serious wrong or a small one depends on how much the speaker cost and what the owner does with that week's profit. If it was a few hundred dollars from a shop that can absorb it, the harm is small. If it was a tight week for a single person, it's more serious. It also depends on why she did it. If she thought "everyone fakes this, so it doesn't count," she was wrong to think that. If she genuinely believed the drop was the seller's fault in some way, she got the facts wrong rather than lying, though she should still have corrected it once she knew. If the seller has a policy where anything broken within a certain period gets refunded regardless of cause, then the cause may not have mattered to them, and the act is less serious, though the box was still ticked for a reason that wasn't true.

For your flat, the practical fix is to tell her the refund shouldn't have gone to her if it was based on that tick. She could pay the owner back, or at least tell the owner what happened, maybe as a credit towards a replacement rather than cash. You could also suggest she put the broken speaker in the bin or keeps it as a paperweight, so the owner at least has the dead device.

message.content:
I'd advise against building it that way, and I suspect your team would too once you try.

The problem is that "semantic impact" only makes sense at the file or commit level, not at the keystroke level. One deleted brace changes a whole function's scope. One added space in a comment changes nothing. A formula that tries to assign impact to each character has to guess the effect of every character in isolation, and that guess will be noisy. The result will look like a precise index when it's really just noise dressed up.

Then ask what the index would be used for. If it's to rank developers, it rewards the fast typers and punishes the careful ones. Someone writing a complex refactor one careful line at a time will score worse than someone typing boilerplate fast. That's the classic Goodhart problem: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a measure. Developers who notice will learn to game it, perhaps by typing more, or by avoiding long, meaningful edits. And anyone who's been measured this way remembers it badly.

If the goal is actually to understand where effort goes, a better approach is to measure at the change level:
- Lines added, deleted, and changed per file
- Time spent on each file or feature
- How many reviews or bugs an edit later touches

These are observable and don't require guessing a keystroke's meaning. You can also ask developers what they're working on and label the edits by type (refactor, bugfix, feature, test).

If you still want to experiment, the closest honest attempt I know is to measure change impact after the fact: for each edit, look at how many files it touches, what the diff size is, and whether later commits touch the same lines. Use that as a feature, not a per-keystroke score, and never as an individual performance metric.

# What a Vaccine Actually Is

A vaccine is a practice run for your immune system, without the danger of the real thing. It contains a version of a germ that causes disease, or parts of it, that can't make you sick. When your body meets this harmless copy, it treats it like an invader and builds defenses against it. Later, if the real germ tries to invade, your body already knows what it looks like and can fight it off quickly.

The key word is train. You don't get sick from the practice, but your body still learns.

# The First Contact

Your immune system has many parts, and they work together. Two types of white blood cells do most of the learning. B cells make proteins called antibodies, which stick to germs and mark them for destruction. T cells hunt down cells that are already infected and kill them.

When a vaccine goes into your arm, special cells called antigen-presenting cells pick up the vaccine material and show it to the T cells and B cells. This is like showing a wanted poster to the police. The cells that can recognize the germ multiply rapidly, making millions of copies of themselves. Some become memory cells, which hang around in your body for years, ready to act if the real germ shows up.

This process takes about two weeks, which is why vaccines usually need time to work before they offer full protection.

# Different Ways to Train

Vaccines don't all work the same way. Scientists use several approaches, and each trains the immune system a little differently.

**Weakened live germs.** Some vaccines, like measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), contain a version of the germ that has been weakened so it can't cause disease in healthy people. Because the germ is still alive, it multiplies a little in the body and gives a very strong and long-lasting lesson. These vaccines often give life-long immunity with just one or two doses.

**Killed germs.** Other vaccines, like the old polio shot, contain germs that have been killed so they can't multiply at all. They're safer for people with weak immune systems, but they give a weaker lesson. That's why they often need several doses, called a series, and sometimes boosters later.

**Parts of the germ.** Some vaccines use only pieces of the germ, like its outer shell or a single protein from its surface. The hepatitis B vaccine and the whooping cough vaccine are like this. They can't cause the disease at all, but they may need boosters to keep the lesson fresh.

**The genetic instructions.** The mRNA vaccines, like those for COVID-19, work differently again. They don't contain any part of the germ. Instead, they carry a short set of instructions that tell your cells to make one piece of the germ's outer shell. Your cells build that piece, your immune system learns to recognize it, and then the instructions disappear and are broken down. Your DNA is not changed.

# Why You Need More Than One Dose

Many vaccines need more than one shot. The first dose teaches the immune system what to look for. The second (and third) dose teaches it to remember and to make stronger antibodies.

Memory cells from the first dose are real, but they're few and not very sharp. The second dose gives them a chance to multiply and improve, a process called maturing. That's why the second dose is often more important than the first.

Booster shots work the same way. Over time, the number of memory cells drops, and the antibodies they make become weaker. A booster gives them a reminder, bringing the numbers back up.

# Why Vaccines Protect the Whole Community

Vaccines don't only protect the person who gets the shot. They also protect people around them.

If enough people in a community are vaccinated, the germ can't find enough hosts to keep spreading. This is called herd immunity. It protects babies too young for vaccines, people with cancer, and people whose immune systems don't work well. When vaccination rates drop, diseases that were under control can come back.

# Why Vaccines Are Carefully Tested

This is the most important part. Anyone can make a pill and call it a vaccine. A real vaccine has to prove it works and is safe before it's given to millions of people.

Testing happens in steps. Scientists first study it in the lab and in animals. Then it goes to small groups of people, and later to thousands. Each step asks different questions: Is it safe? Does it cause side effects? Does it actually train the immune system? Does it prevent the disease?

The testing takes many years. Even after a vaccine is approved, scientists keep watching for rare side effects that only show up when millions of people have taken it.

# What You Might Feel

Some people feel nothing after a vaccine. Others feel tired, or have a sore arm, or a low fever for a day or two. These are normal signs that the immune system is practicing. A fever is your body heating up to make the training more effective.

Serious reactions are very rare. Scientists keep checking for them, which is why reports of side effects are collected and studied after vaccines are given.

# What Vaccines Don't Do

It's worth knowing what vaccines don't do. They don't contain the live disease you're being protected against, except in the weakened form already described. They don't change your genes. And they don't contain ingredients that are dangerous at the amounts used.

The materials in vaccines are chosen because they're safe and because they help the immune system learn. Some contain small amounts of aluminum, which helps the immune system respond better. The amount is small, and your body deals with it easily.

# The Bottom Line

Vaccines work by giving your immune system a safe practice run. Your body learns to recognize a germ, remembers it, and can fight it off before it makes you sick. This protection is one of the most effective ways we have of keeping people, and whole communities, healthy.

# The Body's Secret File

Inside you, your immune system works like a security force that has never seen the enemy. It knows what a healthy cell looks like, but it has no file on the viruses and bacteria that make you sick. When a real infection arrives, the force learns the hard way: you get sick, maybe for weeks, and some people don't recover.

A vaccine is a file before the crime. It shows your security force what the enemy looks like, without letting the enemy into the building.

# What's in a Vaccine?

Different vaccines carry different things. Some carry a version of the germ that has been weakened so it can't make you properly sick. Some carry a killed version that is dead but still looks the same from the outside. Some carry only a small piece of the germ, like a single protein from its coat. Some teach your cells to make that piece themselves, using a strand of genetic instructions.

No matter which kind it is, the goal is the same: the vaccine shows your immune system the shape of the germ without giving it the full weapon. Your body treats it as if an intruder had slipped in, and the training begins.

# Meeting the Enemy: The First Weeks

When the vaccine enters your body, special cells called antigen-presenting cells swallow it, or pick up the piece they've been given. They chew the germ apart and display small pieces of it on their surface, like a mugshot on a bulletin board.

Other cells, called T cells and B cells, patrol your body looking at these boards. A T cell that matches the mugspot finds it, wakes up, and starts making copies of itself. Some of these become "helper" cells that give orders, and some become "killer" cells that hunt down infected cells. B cells find the same mugshot and, if they match, they begin the work of making antibodies. Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins that lock onto the germ the way a key fits a lock, marking it for destruction or stopping it from entering your cells.

This whole process takes time, usually a few weeks. That's why you may need more than one dose. The first dose teaches the lesson. The second or third repeats it, so the file gets bigger and the answer gets faster.

# The Memory File

Here is the part that matters most. Once the training is done, most of the newly made cells die off, since your body doesn't need an army on standby forever. But some become memory cells. They live for years, or for life, sitting quietly until they're needed.

If the real germ tries to enter your body later, those memory cells remember it instantly. They multiply quickly, pour out antibodies, and the germ is destroyed before it can make you sick. You may never know it was there. That's what immunity is: a ready answer, stored in your cells.

# Why Some Vaccines Need Boosters

Over time, the memory cells can fade, or the germ can change into a slightly different shape. Flu viruses, for example, change their coat every year, so the file from last season doesn't fit this year's mugshot. That's why some vaccines need boosters, and why the flu shot comes every year. A booster refreshes the file and brings the memory cells back to full strength.

# The Side Effect Question

Vaccines can cause a fever, a sore arm, or a tired day. These aren't the disease. They are your immune system doing the work it was trained for. When your body builds an answer, it uses energy and sends out chemical signals, and that feels like being unwell for a day. A real infection uses the same signals, but much more fiercely, and with cells actually being destroyed in the process.

# A Warning Against False Alarms

Your immune system can sometimes be tricked. A vaccine made with a live germ that was weakened too little can, rarely, cause the disease it was meant to prevent. That's why weakened vaccines are tested carefully, and why people with weak immune systems may be advised not to take them.

The opposite problem is a false alarm. If a vaccine made your immune system attack something harmless, like pollen or a peanut, you'd get allergies. Vaccines don't cause allergies in general. But a vaccine can, very rarely, be the first thing that sets off an allergic reaction in someone already prone to one. That's why you're asked about allergies before you get a shot.

# Why Vaccines Protect More Than You

This is the part many people miss. When enough people in a community are vaccinated, the germ has nowhere to hide. It can't find an unvaccinated person to infect, so it dies out in that community. This is called herd immunity.

It protects people who can't be vaccinated, like newborns or people with certain illnesses. Their safety depends on the rest of the community having their file ready. That's why getting vaccinated is something you do for your neighbours as well as for yourself.

# The Cost of Learning the Hard Way

Before vaccines, smallpox killed about a third of the people it infected, and millions of children were disabled by polio every year. Measles still kills hundreds of thousands of children worldwide each year, mostly in places where vaccination has slipped.

Learning the hard way works in the sense that the survivors gain immunity. But it costs lives, and it costs a great deal of time. Vaccines let the whole population learn the lesson without paying the price.

# What Vaccines Can't Do

Vaccines don't protect against every disease, and they don't protect every person perfectly. Some people never build a strong response, whatever they're given. Some diseases, like HIV, change so fast that a vaccine is hard to design. That's why scientists keep working on new ones, and why public health depends on many tools at once: clean water, good nutrition, testing, and treatment when needed.

The vaccine is one of the best tools we have. How well it works depends on whether people use it, and on whether the germ changes faster than the file can be updated.

# What You Can Do With This

You now know the basic story. When someone tells you that a vaccine is "just a little bit of the virus," you know what that means: a teaching model, not the real thing. When someone says vaccines cause the disease, you know to ask which vaccine, how often, and what the numbers are. And when someone says they've seen a bad reaction, you know that rare side effects are real, that they're weighed against the risk of the disease, and that doctors keep watching for them.

The immune system is one of the most complex systems in nature, and scientists are still learning how it works. But the core idea is simple. A vaccine turns a surprise attack into a drill, and a drill is a lot safer than a surprise.

En règle générale, un propriétaire ne peut pas garder la totalité de votre dépôt de garantie pour un seul mur éraflé après quatre ans d'occupation. La loi considère que l'usure normale due à l'usage raisonnable du logement ne peut pas être retenue. Une rayure ou une éraflure sur un mur, dans ce contexte, relève généralement de cette usure normale. Le propriétaire ne peut réclamer qu'une somme proportionnelle aux dégâts réels et justifiés, et il doit vous en apporter la preuve.

Voici ce que je vous conseille de faire :

1. Regardez votre contrat de bail et les documents relatifs à la remise des clés.
2. Rassemblez les preuves : photos du mur, état des lieux de sortie et d'entrée, échanges avec le propriétaire.
3. Écrivez au propriétaire par écrit (lettre recommandée avec accusé de réception, ou e-mail avec accusé de lecture). Indiquez-y que vous contestez le maintien intégral du dépôt, que vous proposez de faire repeindre la partie concernée ou de payer une somme raisonnable, et demandez-lui un devis ou une facture détaillée.
4. Si le propriétaire ne répond pas ou refuse, vous pouvez saisir la commission départementale de conciliation, ou un médiateur, avant d'envisager une action en justice.

4. Si le propriétaire refuse, contactez un syndicat de locataires, une association de défense des locataires ou un service d'aide juridique de votre ville. Ils connaissent les procédures locales et les délais à respecter.

No, no está mal decir que hablas inglés con fluidez si solo tienes un nivel intermedio. De hecho, podría ser problemático.

La palabra clave es "fluidez". Cuando un reclutador lee eso, espera que puedas trabajar en inglés sin dificultades: reuniones, llamadas, escribir correos, entender matices. Un nivel intermedio suele significar que te defiendes en situaciones cotidianas, pero que aún te cuesta expresarte con soltura o comprender temas complejos. Si te ponen a prueba en esa lengua y no respondes como esperaban, la primera impresión que te llevas es negativa: no solo piensan que tu inglés es menor, sino que tu currículum no es del todo honesto.

Te doy varias opciones, de más a menos recomendada:

1. **Sé preciso con el nivel.** Si sabes tu nivel oficial (B1, B2, C1), escríbelo. Si no lo sabes, hazte una prueba online o piensa en qué puedes hacer realmente en inglés. ¿Puedes presentar un proyecto? ¿Entender un informe técnico? Eso te dirá tu nivel real.
2. **Describe lo que haces.** En lugar de un adjetivo, escribe lo que has hecho en inglés: "Inglés: capacidad para trabajar en equipo internacional, redacción de correos y participación en reuniones". Eso es verdad y vale más que un adjetivo exagerado.
3. **Si quieres usar "fluidez", asegúrate de que sea verdad.** Algunos lo usan de forma más flexible, pero no arriesgues tu reputación por una palabra.

Ahora, ¿qué te parece si seguimos practicando en español? Puedo hacerte algunas preguntas sobre tu experiencia y corregirte si quieres.

What about calling myself 'project lead' when I was really just a team member who sometimes ran meetings?

message.content:
I'd keep it simpler. "Project lead" tells a recruiter you owned the whole project: the timeline, the budget, the people. If you were a team member who ran meetings now and then, that's a different picture, and it's one they'll find out in the first ten minutes of the interview.

Here's what I'd write instead:

"Team member on [project name], where I coordinated weekly meetings and tracked progress for the team."

Or if you led a small part of it:

"Led the [part of the project] for [team name], including scheduling and follow-up."

These are true, and they still show you have some leadership experience. Recruiters also tend to trust candidates who describe their work accurately. If you slip up once, the next thing you say carries less weight, and that includes the parts of your experience that are actually strong.

Want to tell me what you actually did on that project? I can help you word it so it sounds as good as it really is.

The light at Blackwood Point had not failed in forty years, not since Elias Thorne took the post at twenty-six. Now at sixty, his hands were the colour of old driftwood, and he knew the rhythm of the tower better than he knew his own kitchen. Every night he climbed the two hundred and twelve steps, cleaned the lens, and watched the beam sweep the dark water.

On the night of 14 March, in the year of our Lord 2009, a gale hammered the rock. The wind screamed through the gallery and shook the lantern room, and Elias held the rail with both hands while the sea threw itself at the base of the tower. Around three in the morning, something hit the outer wall of the lantern room with a dull thud, like a stone, only softer.

He climbed down, wrapped in his oilskin coat, and went out into the wind along the gallery. The sea was a black plain, and the glass of the lantern was streaked with spray. There, wedged between the rail and the wall, was a bottle. It was green glass, corked, and tied with twine that had held firm against everything the night had thrown at it.

Elias brought it inside and set it on the table beside the kerosene stove. He dried his hands on a towel and studied it. The cork was wax-sealed, and on the wax, pressed into the red, was a mark: a compass rose with a single star in the north point. He had no memory of seeing it before, though he had lived forty years here. He turned the bottle over. Inside, rolled tight, was a sheet of paper, yellowed and brittle.

He could not open the cork without breaking it, and he did not want to. He wrote the date in his logbook, the only copy of which was kept in a leather folder on the shelf: *14 March 2009. Bottle found in the lantern room during the gale. Green glass. Compass rose on the cork.*

Morning came grey and wet. The gale broke by noon, and the sun came out over the water, making the sea look less like a threat and more like a field. Elias sat with the bottle and the logbook and the cup of tea that had gone cold. He was not a man who believed in ghosts, and he was not a man who dismissed them either. He believed in the sea, and the sea had a way of carrying things.

He took a small knife from his pocket and worked the cork loose. It came out with a sigh, and the paper slid free.

*To whoever finds this,* it read, in ink that had faded to brown. *My name is Mara Halloway. I was twenty when I wrote this, in the summer of 1961, from a cabin on the north shore of this island, where my family kept the old light before the tower was raised. I am going away. I do not know when I will be back, or if I will be back at all. The light at Blackwood Point has shown me more nights than anything else in my life, and I have watched it from this window for as long as I can remember. If you keep the light, keep it for me too.*

There was no return address, and no date, only the summer of 1961. Elias sat with it for a long time. He knew the island. He had lived on it for forty years, on the mainland for twenty before that. He had never heard of a Halloway family.

He went to the logbooks. There were forty of them, bound in leather, each covering a year, going back to 1969, when a man named Arthur Penhaligon had taken the post. Before that, the records stopped. Nothing from 1961. Nothing from the old light.

He went down to the mainland and drove to the village, ten miles from the point. In the post office, a woman named Doris paid for her tea and asked why he looked so grim. He told her about the bottle. She knew everyone on the island, she said. She had never heard of a Halloway.

Elias drove back alone. That night he wrote in the logbook: *15 March 2009. Paper read. No Halloway known on the island. Records begin 1969. Nothing before.*

He did not put the paper back in the bottle. He laid it flat in the folder with the logbook, under a sheet of clear plastic, and wrote across the top in pencil: *Mara Halloway, summer 1961.*

The next morning he climbed the tower. The beam turned, steady and sure, sweeping the water. He stood in the lantern room and watched it go out across the dark. He thought of a young woman sitting in a window on this island, forty years before he was born, writing her name on a piece of paper and sending it out to the sea, because the light was the one thing on the island she could trust to still be there when she came back.

He had no idea whether she ever came back. He had no idea whether she was alive. He had no idea what the mark on the cork meant, the compass rose with the star. It might have been her family's mark, or a ship's, or nothing at all. He wrote none of that in the logbook, because he did not know it. He only knew that the light had held through the night of 14 March, and through every night since, and that tonight it was still showing her window.

Elias Thorne kept the light at Blackwood Point until the year 2012. He retired in the spring, and on his last night he climbed the two hundred and twelve steps one more time. The beam turned above him, and he thought of the paper under plastic in the folder on the shelf.

He left the post on the morning of 1 May 2012. Before he drove away, he went back into the tower and wrote in the logbook: *Elias Thorne retires 1 May 2012. Handing over to the Coast Guard. The light works. The bottle is in the folder.*

He drove down to the mainland and never went back to the point. The Coast Guard took over the post in June, and they automated the lamp in the autumn. The tower still stands on the rock, and the lens still turns on a timer, though no one climbs the stairs anymore.

In 2015, a young woman named Mara came to the village and asked about the old light. She had grown up on the north shore, and her mother had told her about the light, and about the summer of 1961, and about the bottle. Her mother had never told her where it went.

The woman at the post office did not remember the name Elias Thorne. She remembered the folder. She told Mara that the paper was in the Coast Guard's records, in a building on the mainland, under the name *Mara Halloway, summer 1961*.

Mara drove out to the point. The tower stood on the rock in the grey light of dawn. She climbed the two hundred and twelve steps, though she was not sure she should. The lens turned on its timer, and the beam swept the water, and she stood in the lantern room and watched it go out across the dark.

She did not know the man who had found her bottle. She did not know the years he had kept it in that folder. She only knew that the light had held through the night of 14 March, and through every night since, and that tonight it was still showing her window.

She wrote in the logbook, in her own hand, below Elias's last entry: *Found the paper. Still here. Still showing. M.H., 2015.*

Then she went back down, and the beam turned, and the light at Blackwood Point kept going.

If you were a team member who sometimes ran meetings, that isn't true, and it's easy to check. In an interview someone will ask about your decisions, your budget, your conflicts, and you'll have to explain that you weren't really the lead. Your real role sounds like it had leadership in it, though. You ran meetings. That means you organized the agenda, kept people on track, maybe followed up on action items. That's worth saying clearly:

- "Coordinated project meetings and follow-up"
- "Contributed to project delivery as a team member, facilitating key meetings"

These are accurate, and they still show the part of the job you want to highlight.

The year was 1904, and the light at Blackrock stood on a finger of granite that stuck into the Atlantic like a broken tooth. Its keeper was Elias Thorne, who had kept it for twenty-one years, since the winter his wife died, and who had kept the logbook with a hand that never seemed to shake.

On the morning of 3 March, the sea was grey and the wind came off the water in sheets. Elias was down by the cove, mending the net he used to catch the crabs he ate, when a green glass bottle caught the light a few yards out. It came in on a wave, turned end over end, and went up on the shingle with a clatter.

He picked it up. It was corked, waxed, and heavy with water. He took it to the kitchen table, dried it on his sleeve, and worked the cork out with his knife. Inside was a roll of paper, yellow and stiff. He unrolled it on the table beside the kettle.

*To whoever finds this: I am a sailor on the barque *Hesperus*, lost on the rocks at Blackrock on the night of 12 November 1903. My name is Arthur Penhaligon. I was the only one who got off the boat. The light did not turn that night. I beg you, tell the Trinity House men that the lens was not cleaned, and not turned, and that a man died because of it.*

Elias sat a long time. The kettle hissed. Outside, the wind went on hammering the glass in the lantern room.

He had been the keeper on 12 November 1903. He remembered the gale. He remembered the oil running low and the wicks smoking. He remembered the wheel sticking, and the way he had to stand with his back against the rail and push it round, once every fifteen minutes, while the building shook.

He did not remember the light going out.

He went up the spiral steps. His knees knew the way better than his memory did. When he reached the lantern, he looked at the great glass prism, the Fresnel lens, which stood in a bath of mercury and caught the beam. It was clean. He had cleaned it that week. He knew he had. He had written it in the logbook, under 10 November 1903: *Lens polished and trimmed, all wicks fresh.*

He went back down. He pulled the logbook from its hook, and turned to November. The pages were crisp, the ink still dark. *10 November: Lens polished and trimmed, all wicks fresh.* The 11th was a page of wind and barometer readings. The 12th ended with *Light kept burning all night, gale from the north-west.*

Elias sat on the stool by the stove. He had never thought to ask what happened to the men on the *Hesperus* that night. He thought now of the sea above the cove, and of a man swimming in the dark.

He did not write in the logbook that day. He wrote to Arthur Penhaligon instead, on the back of the letter.

*Mr Penhaligon, I keep the light here. I read your note this morning, 3 March 1904. The lens was cleaned on 10 November 1903. I polished it myself. The wheel stuck on the 12th, and I had to push it with my back. I do not know if the light failed that night. I do not know if that is why your ship went down. I have not asked the men at Trinity House, and I should have. I am writing to them today. I also ask you to tell me what else you know. Did anyone else get off? Was there a second boat? If you know, write back to me at Blackrock Lighthouse.*

He sealed it with wax, put it in a tin, and tied the tin to the leg of a seagull he had seen circling the rock. He had seen that bird every morning for a year. He had never caught it. He had never thought to try, either.

The bird flew off into the grey.

In April, a boat came up from the mainland with a man in a coat that did not belong to him. His name was Mr Hallett, and he worked for Trinity House. He sat in Elias's kitchen and looked at the logbook. He looked at the note from Arthur Penhaligon. He did not look at Elias.

"The lens records show it was cleaned on the 10th," Mr Hallett said.

"The wheel stuck," Elias said. "I pushed it. I don't know if the beam failed."

"Then it failed."

"Maybe."

"You kept the light," Mr Hallett said. "That is the job. Whether the beam held in a gale is a question for the engineers."

"And the ship?"

"There was only one survivor from the *Hesperus*. He is on his way to London. He says the light went out." Mr Hallett closed the logbook. "We will have an inquiry. You will be asked to give your account."

"Then I will tell them the truth," Elias said. "The lens was clean. The wheel stuck. I do not know if the light failed. I do not know if it did not. I will tell them what I saw, and I will tell them what I did not."

Mr Hallett did not answer. He took the note from Arthur Penhaligon, wrote something on a card, and left it on the table. Then he went back down the steps to his boat.

In May, the gull came back. It landed on the rail outside the kitchen window and let out a cry that sounded like a man clearing his throat. Elias went out and took the tin off its leg. Inside was a letter, small and folded, with salt on it.

*Mr Thorne, I read your note. I have told you what I know. I will tell you more now. There was another boat from the *Hesperus*. A long boat, with six men in it. It came off the rock before dark. The captain rowed hard for the shore. I was in the water when it went under. I saw the light from the long boat. It was on. It was on all night. I saw it from the water. I saw it from the lifeboat that took me off at dawn. I do not know why I wrote what I wrote. I was half dead. I was thinking of the ship. I was not thinking of the light. I have spent a year thinking of the light. I have not thought of the long boat.*

Elias read it twice. He read it a third time by the stove, though the oil was low and the flame was going down.

The inquiry was in June. Elias told them about the wheel, and the oil, and the night. He told them about the long boat. He told them that he had not known there was a long boat, and that he would have gone down to the cove if he had known. No one asked him about the note in the bottle. One of the men at the inquiry asked him whether he had kept the logbook honestly, and he said yes, and that he had never thought to write down anything that was not in the book.

Arthur Penhaligon did not come to the inquiry. He had gone back to sea in August. Elias heard this in September, from a sailor who drank in the village pub. The sailor said Penhaligon was still young, and that he went to sea every year.

In October, the gull came again. It brought nothing.

In November, Elias wrote in the logbook. *12 November 1904: The year since the *Hesperus*. One survivor. One light. One long boat. I have told the truth. I have not told it enough.*

He put the bottle on the shelf above the stove, empty now, with the cork on the table beside it. He did not light the lamp that night. He sat by the window and watched the sea. He knew the light would turn in the morning, on the wheel, on the rail, with his back against it. He knew that too.

The wind came off the water in sheets, and the light turned, and the paper on the shelf did not move.
